source.title: Polysemy of Synthetic Neurons Towards a New Type of Explanatory Categorical Vector Spaces
source.authors: Michael Pichat; William Pogrund; Paloma Pichat; Judicael Poumay; Armanouche Gasparian; Samuel Demarchi; Martin Corbet; Alois Georgeon; Michael Veillet-Guillem

record.tranche_reason: The study measures categorical proximity and activation in GPT2-XL neurons, using a different method from the original neuron examples to test how apparent polysemy relates to activation level.
record.gate_note: The study's own measurements and analyses of GPT2-XL layer 1 are recorded below. Cited findings from other studies and the authors' earlier work are not rows.
record.test_reason: Using GPT2-XL layer-1 MLP neurons, the study asks whether a neuron's core tokens look more categorically homogeneous at the top of its activation range than lower down. Homogeneity is scored as embedding cosine proximity to taken-clusters. This bears on V7, whether polysemanticity depends on which activation range is examined. It does not estimate how common polysemantic neurons are (V2), test causes (V3, V4) or compare architectures (V5).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that token activation is positively and monotonically related to proximity to a neuron's categorical sub-dimensions: high-activation tokens converge (relative monosemy), lower ones diverge (polysemy). They propose a polysemantic neuron is an intra-neuronal categorical vector space with a non-orthogonal basis. They explicitly frame this as an alternative to superposition accounts that does not contradict them, not as a refutation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses GPT2-XL core tokens, embedding cosine similarities, shared-token clusters, and statistical analyses of activation and categorical proximity. It does not use the original sources' neuron-image examples or SoLU method.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured relationship varies with activation rank/range: the study contrasts the 10 least and most activated core tokens, and reports correlations across ranked core tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: In an averaged layer-1 neuron, proximities to its four taken-cluster sub-dimensions are mostly positively correlated (factor 1, 93.5% of variance). A minor factor (4.8%) contrasts the sub-dimensions, ordered by cluster size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The categorical sub-dimensions a neuron inherits from its strongest precursor neurons largely overlap, forming a non-orthogonal basis, with a minor divergent component.

record.problems: The evidence is limited to GPT2-XL layer 1 and selected neurons meeting taken-cluster criteria. The dimensional-proximity measure is based on cosine similarity of GPT2-XL input embeddings, not a direct test of which features the model functionally uses. Several results use an averaged neuron, and the reported mean proximity difference is described as small; only 22.8% of neurons met the stated local significance criterion.

untested.parts: How explanations are scored. No explanation-scoring methods are compared; homogeneity is measured only via input-embedding cosine similarity. Activation ranges below the top 100 core tokens were not examined.
Not tested: no share of polysemantic neurons and no layer comparison. Only layer 1 is analysed despite the summary's mention of the first two layers.
Not tested: the study does not show that canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature, or that unrelated mixtures are rare.
Superposition is discussed only as an alternative framework, not tested.

missing.what: Per-neuron (non-averaged) PCA correlation circles, reported only qualitatively as confirming the averaged pattern. This would let researchers check whether the averaged-neuron results (R2–R7) hold per neuron.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemy is operationalised as embedding-cosine heterogeneity relative to taken-clusters, which are themselves built from core tokens. This is an indirect, circular-prone measure. Results come from selected neurons and mostly from averaged neurons, with no controls or random baselines. The Graph 1 caption appears mismatched (it refers to layer 0 clusters). Findings from the authors' earlier work, such as categorical divergence and convergence, are cited only and are correctly not rows. In the record, V2 and V6 are not supported by any row, so their labels were dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The study analyzes one GPT2-XL MLP layer, not differences across layers or models. It does not estimate the share of all neurons that respond to unrelated inputs; its categorical-proximity measure is not a direct count of unrelated tokens or contexts.
The study discusses superposition as another account but does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization, training noise, and whether polysemanticity occurs without capacity pressure.
Activation-function, architecture, or regularization comparisons, including SoLU, modern convnets, and performance costs.

The study finds greater categorical convergence among the highest-activation tokens, but does not establish that a neuron detects one shared feature actually used by the network, or estimate how rare truly unrelated mixtures are.
The study varies activation rank/range within core tokens. It does not compare explanation-scoring methods or other measures of polysemanticity.

rows.subject: GPT2-XL (aggregate over 614 layer 1 neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean dimensional-proximity scores for each neuron's 10 least- and 10 most-activated core tokens.

conditions.value: 614; each had at least 3 taken-clusters, each with at least 6 taken-tokens, and at least 40 distinct tokens across clusters
100 core-tokens per neuron; compared 10 min and 10 max

rows.measure: Difference in mean dimensional proximity (δ = smax − smin), sign of the difference across neurons, and local significance rate.
rows.baseline: Equiprobability distribution hypothesis for the sign test; otherwise not stated.
rows.value: Mean δ = .0274; 78.0130% of neurons had δ > 0; % of (PKW (δ > 0) < .05) = 22.8013%; mean Δc = .2407. Mean αmin = 1.3843; mean αmax = 3.0218; mean σmin = .3991; mean σmax = .4265.
rows.note: The authors describe the mean difference as not large, though meaningful; only 22.8% of neurons had a locally significant difference by the stated Kruskal-Wallis criterion.
rows.check: Only V7 applies. No row measures the share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs (V2), or shows that apparent mixtures share one feature (V6). The direction holds in 78% of neurons, but mean δ = .0274 is called 'not large'. Only 22.8% of neurons reach local significance. Range is limited to the top 100 core tokens, and neurons were selected by taken-cluster criteria.

rows.subject: GPT2-XL (average neuron across 612 layer 1 neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Calculated Kendall correlations between activation rank and mean proximity to each of three categorical sub-dimensions.

conditions.value: 612, each with exactly 3 taken-clusters of at least 6 tokens

rows.measure: Kendall's τ between token activation rank and dimensional proximity.
rows.note: The table reports correlations for an average neuron constructed from the selected neurons.
rows.check: Only V7 applies. τ is computed on an averaged neuron of 612 neurons, which likely inflates the correlation relative to individual neurons. Proximity is embedding cosine similarity to taken-clusters, not an explanation score.

rows.subject: GPT2-XL (average neuron across 463 layer 1 neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Conducted PCA on mean token proximity to four categorical sub-dimensions.

conditions.value: 463, each with exactly 4 taken-clusters of at least 6 tokens
PCA of 100 mean core-token ranks by 4 mean dimensional-proximity variables

rows.measure: Variance explained and correlation pattern among the four categorical sub-dimensions.
rows.value: Eigenvalue VP1 = 3.74; factor 1 explained 93.5% of initial variance; all four sub-dimensions were positively correlated with one another.
rows.note: The authors interpret factor 1 as partial categorical convergence and relative monosemy.
rows.check: This PCA describes how the four sub-dimension proximity variables correlate in an averaged neuron. It is not a rate of polysemantic neurons (V2), and not evidence that mixtures reduce to one shared feature (V6). Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: GPT2-XL (average neuron across 463 layer 1 neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Conducted PCA on mean token proximity to four categorical sub-dimensions.

conditions.value: 463, each with exactly 4 taken-clusters of at least 6 tokens
PCA of 100 mean core-token ranks by 4 mean dimensional-proximity variables

rows.measure: Variance explained and contrast among categorical sub-dimensions.
rows.value: Eigenvalue VP2 = .19; factor 2 explained 4.8% of initial variance and contrasted some sub-dimensions; sub-dimension 4 stood apart from the others on the factorial plane.
rows.note: The authors interpret this lower-variance factor as evidence of neuronal polysemy and categorical divergence.
rows.check: The second PCA factor (4.8% of variance) is interpreted by the authors as polysemy. It does not measure how often neurons respond to unrelated tokens. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: GPT2-XL (average neuron across 463 layer 1 neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Projected mean token activation levels onto the PCA factorial axes associated with categorical sub-dimensions.

conditions.value: 463, each with exactly 4 taken-clusters of at least 6 tokens

rows.measure: Association of activation level with positions on the categorical-proximity PCA axes.
rows.value: The text reports that higher-activation tokens had the highest positive values on factor 1 and highest negative values on factor 2; the negative segment of factor 2 was positively linked to the proximity variables for the largest taken-clusters and to 3 of 4 sub-dimension variables.
rows.note: The authors conclude that the higher-activation tokens were associated with a larger number of categorical sub-dimensions.
rows.check: This is a qualitative pattern from Graph 4 for the averaged neuron, with no numbers reported. It bears on V7: higher-activation tokens sit at the convergent pole.

relationships.reason: Activation rank correlates strongly with embedding proximity to sub-dimensions (τ .78–.85, R2–R4). Top-activated tokens sit at the convergent pole (R7), so apparent homogeneity depends on the activation range examined.

relation.reason: The study tests its own hypothesis linking activation level to categorical convergence. The authors tie it explicitly to the observation that neurons look monosemantic on top activations and polysemantic lower down.

tranche.reason: Different method (embedding-cosine proximity of core tokens by activation rank) aimed at whether apparent monosemy depends on the activation range.

source_check.notes: All comparisons use only each neuron's 100 top-activating core tokens. The authors say tokens outside the core set might show larger differences. 'Proximity to sub-dimensions' is embedding cosine, and monosemy is the authors' reading of it. Table 2 and Graph 4 are on averaged neurons. Graph 3 shows non-averaged correlation circles with no numbers. Graph 1's caption in the text looks mismatched (layer 0 clusters).

statements.correction: This study: GPT2-XL layer 1. Averaged neuron over 612 neurons with 3 sub-dimensions: Kendall τ .7754/.8384/.8461 between activation rank and mean input-embedding cosine proximity to taken-clusters (R2-R4). Averaged neuron over 463 neurons with 4 sub-dimensions: higher-activation tokens score highest on PCA Factor 1 and most negative on Factor 2 (R7, no numbers). All within the 100 core tokens. Monosemy/polysemy is the authors' interpretation of proximity.
statements.problem: Cites this study's R2, R3, R4 and R7, but neither the 'what' nor the 'conditions' mention GPT2-XL or this study's result. The evidence is an averaged neuron within each neuron's top-100 core tokens, scored by embedding proximity, not by reading top vs lower activations.
Nothing material. The authors call Cliff's delta .2407 'moderate, non-negligible' and expect larger differences outside the core-token set. The row list says R1,R2 but the text cites R2-R4.

statements.correction: GPT2-XL layer 1, 614 neurons: mean δ = .0274 between the 10 most- and 10 least-activated of each neuron's 100 core tokens. δ > 0 in 78.01% of neurons (χ² p < .0001). Cliff's delta .2407. 22.8% locally significant (Kruskal-Wallis). Authors expect larger differences with tokens outside the core set.
statements.problem: 'Top-vs-bottom' leaves out that both groups are inside the neuron's 100 core tokens: the 10 most- vs 10 least-activated of its top 100. The authors say tokens outside the core set could show much stronger differences. Without that, readers would take it as the full activation range.

Nothing wrong about this study. The metadata says 'rows cited from this study: none', but the text cites R1. This study's GPT2-XL averaged-neuron support (R2-R4, R7) is not listed among the activation-range evidence. That is an omission, not an error.
